questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had not been to the Gulf region before, and have mostly/only traveled in North Africa (Tunisia and Egypt, particularly Egypt) so it was an exciting opportunity to travel once more and travel to a part of the Middle East which I had not made acquaintance with in person before.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The university and trip itself was great, I was struggling with some financial issues and was surprised to find the study-visa to be more expensive than I had anticipated (more so than e.g. Egypt), which also meant I probably didn't explore as much as I could and should have, on top of that there were some challenges with getting the necessary Erasmus/Exchange-documents in order, but aside from that the university in Dubai was excellent and I met friendly and helpful people so overall a good if shorter than expected experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Good question. The campus was relatively small and I had been put in contact with a student from AUD already who was very helpful in telling me about transportation system, cost of living, helping me search for accommodation, as well as being a personal connection when I had questions about the campus and such.
A map of the campus would've helped though, like a digital one sent to the mail so you can see which building is which.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I suppose I covered that in the previous question but the first day I had to ask the guard where the "B"-building was, and at one point I had to ask my friend where the "C"-building was to find the administrative offices. Other than that the University was right next to the metro station so that was pretty easy.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: As I said, a map of the campus would be awesome. Even just a basic of "which building is which, and if you have to go see the student affairs offices - here's the main building" or something.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Travel costs add up, and you need to get a NOL-card to travel by bus or metro, so highly recommend upon arrival to find the nearest place to buy a NOL-card, typically on every metro station though I forgot if the Airport metro had one. May also be an idea to look up some of the travel card options, but a NOL-card is absolutely necessary to travel in Dubai if you go by public transport.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was okay, apartments off-campus were a bit expensive, but I was personally not a fan of the house-rules at AUD. They did waiver the curfew-requirements which was great, but it felt a bit restrictive still - which is understandable given both the Emirati and American views on "young people and college students", anyhow rules are rules, but personally I didn't like having visitor-rules and such when I am a 28 year old adult male.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I'd like to give higher and the administration were very friendly, but it was *extremely* confusing. In my case the communication was not super clear and there were often misunderstandings about what had been done and not done, timeschedule was a bit opaque - some moments i felt like deadlines were right around the corner and i was about to be kicked out, and then i later find out that course registrations are accepted (including drop/add periods) up until about a week or two after semester start.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I received mails fairly early on about upcoming application and enrollment, including information about things i had to do (visa, health checkups, enrollments, tuition fees - which i then didnt have to pay anyway because I was an Erasmus student - and their website application form, and later course selections). I dont remember it in detail as it started way back in march or april while I was on exchange in Cairo. But i remember the process felt confusing and it seemed like the contact persons (which also wasnt entirely clear whom i had to report to) were not always up to date on what i had sent and needed to send or action to take.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
They have a university website
aud.edu
with lots of information and forms, although i think it would've been cool for a section of "if you are an exchange student, click here - step by step guide on what you need to do" a bit similar to Mobility Online here, with an easy-to-overview design so you constantly know where you are in the process.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The undergraduate course schedule is invaluable so they should use it for the class registration, and then look up course catalogue for a deeper description of the courses (which matches the course code in the course schedule, use ctrl + F to find the desired code quickly)

As for registration.. im not really sure, be sure to have a spare 10.000 DKK for the visa however, even though no tuition or course fee is paid. IF you are in doubt about whom to contact, I would suggest going directly to Sara L. Montero and either ask her, or ask whom you should contact. She's the dean of student affairs and extremely helpful, and when you do arrive you can go by her office in the C-building(the big building with the cafes and campus-kiosk and everything), unless she's off somewhere she's usually happy to have a conversation with an exchange student, even if you haven't arranged any meeting.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Excellent. Teachers were really good, the exam and grading system obviously different as it goes by the American standard - grades are a mix of final exam and during-course tests and attendance, but by and large the teachers were very competent. The course selections are also cool, as there are unique options that weren't available at UCPH.
They use a platform called "Blackboard" which is the equivalent of "Absalon" used at UCPH, so when they talk about that they dont actually mean a physical blackboard, it took me a few days to realize.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took BA courses but i took at least one course which i THINK might be on MA level if it had been at UCPH, it was a much more advanced macroeconomics course focusing on the financial institutions and monetary system, it was fairly difficult. I also took an arabic class aimed at native arabic speakers which was naturally way above the vocabulary level I was used to, but it was really good anyway. The rest of the courses were pretty standard for what I'd expect at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Much more classroom and lecturing, the lectures are also way shorter(50 minutes per class M/W/F, and 75 minutes tuesdays and thursdays) so we usually didnt have time for in-group work except for the arabic class which sometimes incorporated it. I wouldve liked more of the UCPH style of "you work in groups within the class" whereas AUD was more top-down lecturing with input from students towards the teacher, and some courses featured heavy expectation of solving assignments particularly at home which isn't bad in itself, but it felt both more independent (as you'd have to study more on your own) and simultaneously less in-class capacity for getting the material under your skin. I would have enjoyed more pair/group-work, and maybe also feedback other than just a grade / right-wrong signs from my assignments.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Arabic Proficiency I
Principles of Microeconomics / Principles of Macroeconomics (two courses)
Applied Econometrics
Money & Banking

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I mean it depends on their major and interests, if its arabic students - the arabic proficiency classes are very good to give a vocabulary challenge, I feel like Im fairly good at UCPH - except maybe for grammar - but I got very challenged as it was in an environment of arabic speaking natives, who might be on a similar level with grammar-proficiency but naturally have a much higher vocabulary even in standard arabic which isnt their "mother-tongue" (as most speak dialects) but they still have a better command of the language than me, and it was pretty clear from reading out loud to translation.

Applied Econometrics is a great course for data analysis, it wasnt so heavy on the mathematics of econometrics, but still enough statistics (which is a recommended pre-requisite, that i didnt have though i do have some statistical knowledge) that if you arent from a math background you'll have to study.

The micro/macroeconomics courses are as you can expect and i suppose on a similar level to UCPH, good courses in my opinion but my degree while being within the arts, is turning more towards economic-cultural bridging due to my natural interest in more "social-sciences"-aspects of the MENA region. Unfortunately I didnt try the cultural courses about MENA as i wanted, like mentioned above, due to course-registration conflicts.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Okay so its pretty important to give my personal circumstances: my apartment was probably slightly more expensive than campus-apartments, so the rent could be slightly lower. I also lived almost two hours away by bus and metro, so i paid 50 DKK a day in transportation costs. Food costs was a pretty low end for me as i was trying to save and eat cheaply, living off chicken (which was only like 18 DKK for 400g), noodles, and strawberry milk. The visa costs of 10.000 DKK was a huge surprise, which would include health insurance and such hence the high price. I ended up not paying for internet on my phone as i had wifi in the apartment, mostly to save costs. Otherwise its a few hundred DKK a month i suppose.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Chicken breast was pretty cheap. I shopped at something called Shaklan in International City, only about 9 AED or 18 DKK for a 400g chicken breast. Foreign products, candy, milk and such were fairly expensive but not really worse than Denmark. Overall I maintained a similar budget to Denmark or slightly less, out of my own choice. Eggs were also not too expensive if i remember correctly. 
Some shops/supermarkets like Shaklan is also cheaper than Carrefour, which is otherwise my go-to supermarket chain in MENA. I didnt cook so much myself other than cooking noodles, but they do have a lot of rice and other asian-food since they have so many indians, filipinos, and other asians there. Meat / rice and likely carbs in general were pretty cheap, but its also standard in the Middle East to eat such types of food.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Honestly, there were lots of opportunities but I just failed to make use of them.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
They had sports teams including Badminton areas, Swimming pool, but im unsure if you can just use them or if you have to be part of their sports teams. There were often plastered advertisement on the activity-walls however about things you could apply for (including dancing), and letters were sometimes sent out with news of upcoming events - they also have an instagram page (@audstudentlife)

theres also lots of benches outside to sit at, which was comfortable during the autumn and early winter as the temperatures were temperate (around 20-25C). People were also friendly but i didnt find it as easy being social as in Egypt, but thats probably more to do with me having difficulty being social in general. 

- oh and before i forget, they DO arrange tours to the deserts and such, which would be a fantastic opportunity.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Go on sightseeing trips arranged by the University or someone affiliated with it. If you're a little more social adept than me it might also be possible to go out and enjoy some cafes with friends from the university, but i didnt really manage to do that myself so i dont have a lot of advice. You could try and ask the offices in the C-buildings though or Sara Montero if she has ideas, she's ready to do her part to integrate and give students a good time.

Also ask already before arriving! I was given an exchange student that was supposed (but couldnt get visa) to go to Denmark to study at UCPH and she was a great pen-pal for me. Try and ask AUD if they can make it a practice to offer their students to sign up to be "contact-friends" for incoming exchange students from abroad.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Try and see Palm Jumeira or some of the exciting places in Dubai, I was very constrained financially so mostly I met up with two friends (one saudi and one algerian) coming from abroad, with the former visiting.. I think Hilton Hotel or something around the Jumeira area, it was really cool to visit that place honestly but I didnt have the most luxurious experience due to financial shortage myself.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. I mean the Emirates is obviously culturally different especially with regards to the natives (who wear their traditional clothing, you aren't in doubt). But there are a lot of foreigners, and the UAE is accustomed to being more accommodating of westerners, particularly americans, so honestly i didnt feel much of a difference except i didnt have many "close" people to talk to.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
I never really find a good technique, though they often made contact with me to hear where I am from etc and greeted me in the halls so they were pretty friendly, but arguably it was easier for me to socialise in Egypt as they are naturally more "aggressive" in making friends. But honestly, just try and talk with the guy or girl next to you, i felt they were very friendly even the Emiratis though the girls can be a little more reserved.

My biggest tip though: Get their whatsapp numbers in class, we used it a lot anyway to communicate and coordinate.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Indians (relevant on the metro) have a different concept of personal space than most people in the west. Egyptians also, but i found the indians to be worse. Other than that, my own biggest challenge has been the socialising part. Egypt like i said was easier because they mostly come to you, but the Gulf is more reserved as a far as socialising goes - and "hanging out" with mixed genders is even more difficult. I did make a good female friend there, but we only really talked deeper on a personal level towards the end of the semester, despite talking often on whatsapp throughout the semester since she often had questions regarding economics and such.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
I felt people are very friendly and helpful, in fact I felt a bit sorry for the exchange student who was supposed to come here - because the visa authorities in Denmark were everything but helpful, even though she did everything on time, whereas I was met with a lot of accommodation despite messing up deadlines and such. Unfortunately she didnt get it in time and wasn't able to come, I met her once or twice at AUD in Dubai to say hi.
But definitely the friendliness and respect, I always feel like MENA gives some "white privilege" to westerners, which is heartwarming.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Make sure your finances are in order. I left with around 24.000 DKK (having faced some hardship due to having to lend money to family members the year prior) and it was not enough. Flight, apartment, and rent before you get SU, 1500-3000 DKK for food as well as Visa adds up very quickly. If you can make sure you have at least 40.000.

2. Pretty niche, but i bought books for the courses equivalent to what i was going to study abroad (actually i had bought them the year prior because i knew id be taking those courses anyway at UCPH), buy them at UCPH's library then you can study the courses beforehand. I had chewed through my economics textbook within the first three weeks of the semester, which meant i was pretty well prepared for the course material. Personally i like it that way if i can be well prepared for the course so i can relax more during the semester, this is maybe more related to economics where you already sort of know what you will be studying. 

3. Consider bringing an adapter. Some sockets can be used with our electronic devices, but they do use a different socket standard than Denmark. 

4. Very niche, but install MitID on two devices. My phone broke during my stay and i wasnt able to fix it until i came home because the new phone i had was unable to scan my passport and the local municipality cant issue you a new activation code online/through webcam meeting, so i was effectively locked out of my UCPH mail, Bank access (except for physical card), everything requiring MitID to access.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: hmm.. i wish i had more to say on this but i cant think of any.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: For me, definitely seeing the UAE. I didnt get to see all i wanted, which again the moral of the story is "dont be poor" haha but yeah.. i feel like my trip has been good to sort of getting me acquainted with the area, so if i go again it would be easier to find my way around and go enjoy places sometime later in life. A huge part of it was to simply see the country as I had never been there, and I guess mission complete on that part.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: think i said it more than enough but my skinny bank account. It really put a strain on everything.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
A VPN is useful as the UAE blocks some websites (also most voicechat), and IF you happen to be in a very unfortunate situation where you have to make an online payment and its getting blocked, its likely because of this - use a VPN to get around it. Its not illegal to use, only if you use it for something that actually is illegal.

Also, UAE speaks english for the most part. *rarely* have i had to use arabic to communicate, as most are international and speak english just fine, so dont worry about that.

Other than that, enjoy it.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
